decks.title: Isomerism — Part 1: Structural and geometrical isomerism
goals: Define isomerism and identify chain, position, functional, metamerism and tautomerism among structural isomers
Draw and name the structural isomers of a formula such as C4H10O
State the conditions for geometrical isomerism and draw cis and trans forms of but-2-ene
Distinguish syn and anti forms of oximes

slides.heading: One formula, many compounds
slides.body_md: **Isomers** are compounds with the **same molecular formula** but **different properties**, because their atoms are arranged differently. Part 1 covers **structural** isomers (different connectivity) and **geometrical** isomers (different arrangement in space about a double bond).

visual.alt: Table comparing ethanol and methoxymethane, two isomers of C2H6O, in state, boiling point, reaction with sodium and functional group

slides.narration: Namaste! Two compounds can share a molecular formula and still be very different. Ethanol is a liquid that reacts with sodium. Methoxymethane, with the same atoms, is a gas that does not react with sodium. Such compounds are called isomers, and in this part we classify the ways in which isomers can differ.

slides.heading: Types of isomerism
slides.body_md: **Structural isomerism:** the atoms are joined in a different order (chain, position, functional group, metamerism, tautomerism). **Stereoisomerism:** the order is the same but the arrangement in space differs (geometrical and optical).

nodes.label: Structural: chain, position, functional, metamerism, tautomerism

visual.alt: Flow chart dividing isomerism into structural and stereoisomerism

slides.narration: Isomerism is divided into two broad classes. In structural isomerism the atoms are joined in a different order. There are five kinds: chain, position, functional group, metamerism and tautomerism. In stereoisomerism the atoms are joined in the same order but are arranged differently in space. The two kinds are geometrical and optical isomerism.

slides.heading: Chain, position, functional and metamerism
slides.body_md: **Chain:** different carbon skeletons. **Position:** the same skeleton, a group or bond in a different place. **Functional:** different functional groups. **Metamerism:** different alkyl groups on either side of the same functional group (ethers, ketones, amines).

slides.narration: Here are four kinds of structural isomers. Butane and two methylpropane differ in the carbon chain. Butan one ol and butan two ol have the hydroxyl group in different places. Ethanol and methoxymethane have different functional groups, an alcohol and an ether. Ethoxyethane and one methoxypropane are both ethers with different alkyl groups on the two sides of the oxygen, which is metamerism.

slides.heading: How to recognise each type
slides.body_md: Ask in turn: (1) same functional group? (2) same carbon skeleton? (3) same position of the group? Metamerism needs the same group between different alkyl groups, and is found in compounds with a polyvalent atom or group such as –O–, >C=O or >NH.

visual.alt: Table of four types of structural isomerism with what differs and an example pair

slides.narration: To identify the type of isomerism, ask a few questions in order. Do the two compounds have the same functional group? If not, they are functional isomers. If yes, is the carbon skeleton the same? If not, they are chain isomers. If the skeleton is the same but the group sits in a different place, they are position isomers. And if the same group has different alkyl groups on its two sides, they are metamers.

slides.narration: This is how to find all the isomers of a formula. Take alcohols first. Butane gives butan one ol and butan two ol, and two methylpropane gives two methylpropan one ol and two methylpropan two ol: four alcohols. Then ethers: methoxy propane, ethoxyethane and two methoxypropane, three ethers. In total seven structural isomers.

slides.heading: Worked example: classifying pairs of isomers
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** State the type of isomerism in each pair: (a) pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane; (b) pent-1-ene and pent-2-ene; (c) propanal and propanone; (d) ethoxyethane and 1-methoxypropane.

**Answer.** (a) chain; (b) position (same skeleton, C=C in different places); (c) functional (aldehyde and ketone, both C₃H₆O); (d) metamerism (both ethers, C₄H₁₀O).

visual.alt: Table of four pairs of isomers with their formulas and the type of isomerism

slides.narration: Check each pair. Pentane and dimethylpropane have different carbon skeletons: chain isomers. The two pentenes keep the same skeleton but move the double bond: position isomers. Propanal is an aldehyde and propanone a ketone: functional isomers. And ethoxyethane and methoxypropane are both ethers with different alkyl groups: metamers.

slides.heading: Tautomerism
slides.body_md: **Tautomerism** is a special type of functional isomerism in which two isomers, the **tautomers**, are in **rapid dynamic equilibrium**, usually through the shift of a hydrogen atom. In **keto–enol tautomerism** the carbonyl compound with an α-hydrogen (keto form) shifts a hydrogen from carbon to oxygen to give the enol form (C=C and –OH).

slides.narration: Tautomers are isomers that change into each other quickly and exist together in equilibrium. In keto enol tautomerism, a hydrogen atom moves from the carbon next to the carbonyl group to the oxygen atom, and the double bond moves from carbon oxygen to carbon carbon. For propanone, the keto form overwhelmingly predominates, but the enol form is always present in a tiny amount.

slides.heading: Which compounds show keto–enol tautomerism?
slides.body_md: A compound must have **at least one α-hydrogen**, that is a hydrogen on a carbon next to the C=O group. Ethanal and propanone qualify; methanal (HCHO) and benzaldehyde (C₆H₅CHO) have no α-hydrogen and do not. In ethyl 3-oxobutanoate (ethyl acetoacetate) the enol form is present in a measurable amount.

visual.alt: Table showing which carbonyl compounds have an alpha hydrogen and can show keto-enol tautomerism

slides.narration: Not every carbonyl compound shows this. It needs an alpha hydrogen, a hydrogen on the carbon next to the carbonyl group. Propanone has six and ethanal has three. Methanal, benzaldehyde and dimethylpropanal have none, so they cannot form an enol and show no tautomerism. Ethyl acetoacetate is a famous case where the enol form is easily detected.

slides.heading: Geometrical isomerism: the conditions
slides.body_md: Geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism arises from **restricted rotation** about a double bond (or in a ring). It needs **two different atoms or groups on each doubly bonded carbon**. In the **cis** form the like groups are on the same side; in the **trans** form on opposite sides. The isomers cannot interconvert at room temperature without breaking the π bond.

slides.narration: Because the pi bond stops rotation about a double bond, the groups attached to it are held in place. If each doubly bonded carbon carries two different groups, two arrangements are possible. When the like groups are on the same side, the isomer is cis. When they are on opposite sides, it is trans. The alkene with the double bond at position one in butene has two hydrogens on one carbon, so it has no cis or trans form.

slides.heading: Cis and trans isomers differ in properties
slides.body_md: Geometrical isomers are different compounds with different physical properties. The **cis** form of a 1,2-disubstituted alkene is usually **more polar** (the bond dipoles add) and has the **higher boiling point**; the **trans** form is more symmetrical, packs better and usually has the **higher melting point**.

visual.alt: Table comparing cis and trans 1,2-dichloroethene in dipole moment, boiling point and polarity

slides.narration: In cis one comma two dichloroethene the two carbon chlorine dipoles point to the same side and add up, so the molecule is polar and has the higher boiling point, about three hundred and thirty three kelvin. In the trans form, the dipoles cancel and the dipole moment is zero. The trans isomer boils lower, near three hundred and twenty one kelvin.

slides.heading: Worked example: which alkenes show cis–trans isomerism?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Which of pent-2-ene, but-1-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene and 1,2-dibromoethene show geometrical isomerism?

**Method.** Check the groups on each doubly bonded carbon. Pent-2-ene: C-2 has H and CH₃, C-3 has H and C₂H₅ — **yes**. But-1-ene: C-1 has two H — **no**. 2-Methylbut-2-ene: C-2 has two CH₃ — **no**. 1,2-Dibromoethene: H and Br on each carbon — **yes**.

slides.narration: For each alkene, look at the two groups on each doubly bonded carbon. Pent two ene has a hydrogen and a methyl on one carbon, and a hydrogen and an ethyl on the other, so it has cis and trans forms. But one ene has two hydrogens on one carbon, and two methylbut two ene has two methyl groups on one carbon, so neither does. One two dibromoethene does.

slides.body_md: Rotation about the **C=N** bond of an oxime is also restricted, so oximes show geometrical isomerism. In an **aldoxime** (R–CH=N–OH), the **syn** isomer has the H and OH on the **same side** of C=N; in the **anti** isomer they are on **opposite sides**. (Cis–trans labels are used for C=C; syn–anti for C=N.)

If the hydrogen and the hydroxyl group lie on the same side, we call it the syn form. If they lie on opposite sides, it is the anti form. We use syn and anti for the carbon nitrogen bond and cis and trans for the carbon carbon double bond.

slides.heading: Compounds that turn light
slides.body_md: Part 2 — some compounds rotate the plane of polarised light. This **optical activity** is explained by the **three-dimensional shape** of the molecule.

rows: In every plane at right angles to the ray
Same single plane, turned by an angle α

visual.alt: Table of ordinary light, plane polarised light and light after an optically active solution

slides.narration: Namaste! Ordinary light vibrates in every plane at right angles to its path. Plane polarised light vibrates in one plane only. When plane polarised light passes through some solutions, such as sugar, the plane is turned through an angle. That property is called optical activity, and it tells us about molecular shape.

slides.heading: The Nicol prism
slides.body_md: A **Nicol prism** is a crystal of **calcite** cut along a diagonal and cemented with **Canada balsam**. Unpolarised light splits into an **ordinary (o) ray** and an **extraordinary (e) ray**. The o-ray is **totally reflected** at the balsam layer and absorbed by the blackened face; only the **e-ray**, plane polarised, passes out.

An optically active solution turns the plane through an angle alpha. A second Nicol prism, the analyser, is then turned until the original brightness is restored, and the angle read from the circular scale is the angle of rotation.

slides.heading: Dextro- and laevorotatory; specific rotation
slides.body_md: A substance that turns the plane **clockwise** is **dextrorotatory (d or +)**; **anticlockwise** is **laevorotatory (l or −)**. The observed rotation depends on length of tube, concentration, temperature and wavelength, so chemists quote the **specific rotation** $[\alpha]$: the rotation by a solution of concentration 1 g mL⁻¹ in a tube 1 dm long.

headers: Specific rotation (D line, about 293 K), given

visual.alt: Table of specific rotations of sucrose, glucose and fructose

math: [\alpha] = \frac{\alpha}{l \times c} \qquad (l \text{ in dm},\ c \text{ in g mL}^{-1})
slides.narration: If the plane turns clockwise, as seen looking towards the source, the substance is dextrorotatory, marked d or plus. If it turns anticlockwise, it is laevorotatory, marked l or minus. Because the angle depends on tube length and concentration, we quote the specific rotation, the angle for a one decimetre tube and a concentration of one gram per millilitre.

slides.heading: Worked example: observed rotation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 5.00 g of glucose ([α] = +52.7°) is dissolved in water to make 50.0 mL of solution, which is placed in a 2.00 dm tube. Find the observed rotation.

**Step 1.** $c = 5.00 \div 50.0 = 0.100\ \text{g mL}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** $\alpha = [\alpha] \times l \times c = 52.7 \times 2.00 \times 0.100 = 10.54$, so $\alpha \approx +10.5^\circ$.

visual.alt: Table of concentration, tube length and observed rotation for the glucose example

slides.narration: First find the concentration in grams per millilitre: five grams in fifty millilitres is nought point one grams per millilitre. Then multiply the specific rotation by the tube length in decimetres and by the concentration. Fifty two point seven times two times nought point one gives about ten point five degrees, positive because glucose is dextrorotatory.

slides.heading: Quick check: specific rotation
slides.body_md: Use [α] = α / (l × c) with the tube length in decimetres.
slides.narration: Quick check. Convert the tube length to decimetres and the concentration to grams per millilitre before using the formula.

slides.heading: Worked example: concentration from rotation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A solution of glucose in a 2.00 dm tube rotates the plane by +4.22°. Find its concentration, with [α] = +52.7°.

**Solution.** $c = \dfrac{\alpha}{[\alpha] \times l} = \dfrac{4.22}{52.7 \times 2.00} = 0.04004$, so $c \approx 0.0400\ \text{g mL}^{-1}$, that is 4.00 g in 100 mL.

visual.alt: Table of the given rotation and tube length and the concentration found

slides.narration: The same formula can be turned round to find the concentration. Divide the observed rotation by the product of the specific rotation and the tube length. Four point two two divided by fifty two point seven times two gives about nought point zero four zero zero grams per millilitre, or four grams in a hundred millilitres.

The usual cause is an **asymmetric (chiral) carbon atom**, one bonded to **four different atoms or groups**, marked with an asterisk. A molecule with a plane or centre of symmetry is achiral and inactive.

slides.heading: d and l forms and the racemic mixture
slides.body_md: The **d form** and **l form** rotate by equal angles in opposite directions. An **equimolar mixture** of d and l forms is a **racemic mixture** ((±) or dl). It is **optically inactive by external compensation**: the rotation by the d molecules is cancelled by the l molecules, which are **separate molecules**. It can be separated into the two forms (resolution).

visual.alt: Table of the d form, l form and racemic mixture with rotation and notation

slides.narration: The d and l forms rotate the plane by equal angles in opposite directions. If we mix equal numbers of d and l molecules we get a racemic mixture. Its net rotation is zero, because the rotation caused by the d molecules is cancelled by the l molecules. This is called external compensation, because the cancelling happens between separate molecules.

This is **internal compensation**: the rotation by one half of the molecule is cancelled by the other half **in the same molecule**. A meso compound cannot be resolved into optically active forms.

slides.narration: In a meso compound the molecule itself has a plane of symmetry that divides it into two halves that are mirror images. One half would rotate the plane clockwise and the other anticlockwise by the same amount, so the molecule is inactive. This is internal compensation. Unlike a racemic mixture, a meso compound is a single compound and cannot be separated into optically active forms.

slides.heading: Quick check: the meso form
slides.body_md: Explain why a molecule with chiral carbons can still be inactive.
slides.narration: Quick check. Look for an internal plane of symmetry that makes one half the mirror image of the other.

slides.heading: How many stereoisomers?
slides.body_md: A molecule with **n different chiral carbons** (no symmetry) has **2ⁿ** optical isomers, in n pairs of enantiomers. If the molecule is **symmetrical**, as in tartaric acid, meso forms appear and the number is smaller.

visual.alt: Table of the number of stereoisomers for compounds with one, two and three chiral carbons

slides.narration: With one chiral carbon there are two stereoisomers. If there are two different chiral carbons, with different groups at the two ends, there are four stereoisomers. But if the two ends are the same, as in tartaric acid, a meso form appears and there are only three. With three different chiral carbons there are two to the power three, that is eight.

bullets: Plane-polarised light is obtained from ordinary light with a Nicol prism; a polarimeter measures the angle of rotation α.
Specific rotation $[\alpha] = \alpha / (l \times c)$, with $l$ in dm and $c$ in g mL⁻¹.
A chiral molecule (usually with an asymmetric carbon) is optically active; mirror images are enantiomers.
Racemic mixture: equal d and l, inactive by external compensation. Meso: inactive by internal compensation.
Tartaric acid has three stereoisomers; lactic acid has two.

Chiral carbons plus a plane of symmetry: internal compensation

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. A Nicol prism gives plane polarised light, and a polarimeter measures the rotation. The specific rotation is the observed rotation divided by tube length in decimetres and concentration in grams per millilitre. Chiral molecules are optically active. A racemic mixture is inactive because of external compensation, and a meso compound because of internal compensation.

sections.heading: 1. Isomerism and structural isomerism
sections.body_md: **Isomers** have the same molecular formula but different structures and therefore different properties. **Structural isomerism:** **chain** (different carbon skeleton: pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane), **position** (group or multiple bond in a different place: butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol), **functional** (different functional groups: ethanol and methoxymethane; propanal and propanone) and **metamerism** (different alkyl groups on either side of the same group: ethoxyethane and 1-methoxypropane). **Stereoisomerism:** same connectivity, different arrangement in space (geometrical and optical).

key_terms.definition_md: The existence of two or more compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures or arrangements of atoms.
Structural isomerism arising from different alkyl groups on the two sides of a polyvalent functional group such as –O– or >C=O.

sections.heading: 2. All the isomers of C₄H₁₀O; tautomerism
sections.body_md: C₄H₁₀O has **7 structural isomers**: four alcohols (butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol) and three ethers (1-methoxypropane, ethoxyethane, 2-methoxypropane); butan-2-ol also has a mirror-image pair. Work systematically: family, skeleton, position. **Tautomerism:** two isomers in rapid dynamic equilibrium by the shift of a hydrogen atom; in **keto–enol** tautomerism a carbonyl compound with an α-hydrogen (keto) is in equilibrium with an enol (C=C–OH). Propanone: CH₃COCH₃ ⇌ CH₂=C(OH)CH₃, with the keto form predominating. Methanal and benzaldehyde have no α-hydrogen and show none.

key_terms.definition_md: Isomerism in which two forms are in dynamic equilibrium, usually by the shift of a hydrogen atom, as in keto and enol forms.
A hydrogen atom on the carbon next to a carbonyl group.

sections.heading: 3. Geometrical isomerism
sections.body_md: Needs **restricted rotation** (a C=C bond or a ring) and **two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon**. **cis:** like groups on the same side; **trans:** on opposite sides. But-2-ene shows it; but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene do not. Cis and trans isomers differ in physical properties: cis-1,2-dichloroethene is polar (about 1.9 D, boils near 333 K), trans is non-polar (0 D, about 321 K). Of the isomers of C₄H₈ there are 3 structural alkenes and 4 stereoisomers in all. **Syn and anti isomerism** in oximes (C=N): in an aldoxime the syn form has H and OH on the same side of C=N, the anti form on opposite sides.

key_terms.definition_md: Stereoisomerism arising from restricted rotation about a double bond or a ring, giving cis and trans forms.

sections.heading: 4. Plane-polarised light, polarimeter and specific rotation
sections.body_md: Ordinary light vibrates in all planes perpendicular to its path; **plane-polarised light** vibrates in one plane. A **Nicol prism** (calcite cut along a diagonal and cemented with Canada balsam) separates the **ordinary ray**, which is totally reflected and absorbed, from the **extraordinary ray**, which emerges plane polarised. A **polarimeter** (source, polariser, tube, analyser, scale) measures the **angle of rotation** $\alpha$. Clockwise: **dextrorotatory (d, +)**; anticlockwise: **laevorotatory (l, −)**. Specific rotation: $[\alpha] = \alpha / (l \times c)$, with $l$ in dm and $c$ in g mL⁻¹.

key_terms.definition_md: The ability of a substance to rotate the plane of plane-polarised light.
The rotation, in degrees, produced by a solution of concentration 1 g mL⁻¹ in a tube 1 dm long, at a stated temperature and wavelength.

formulas.label: Specific rotation (l in dm, c in g mL⁻¹)

sections.heading: 5. Chirality and the asymmetric carbon
sections.body_md: A molecule is **chiral** if it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image. The usual cause is an **asymmetric (chiral) carbon**, bonded to **four different** atoms or groups (marked *). A molecule with a plane or centre of symmetry is achiral. Examples with one chiral carbon: butan-2-ol, lactic acid, 2-aminopropanoic acid, 3-methylhexane. Propan-2-ol has none (two CH₃ groups). Mirror-image isomers are **enantiomers**: same physical properties, equal rotations in opposite directions.

key_terms.definition_md: A carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups.
A pair of stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

sections.heading: 6. d and l forms, racemic mixture, meso form and compensation
sections.body_md: The **d form** (+) and **l form** (−) rotate by equal angles in opposite directions. An **equimolar mixture** of d and l is a **racemic mixture** (±): inactive by **external compensation** (cancellation between separate molecules); it can be resolved. A **meso compound** has chiral carbons and an internal plane of symmetry: inactive by **internal compensation** (one half of the molecule cancels the other); it cannot be resolved and is a single compound.

key_terms.definition_md: An equimolar mixture of the d and l forms; optically inactive by external compensation.
A compound with chiral carbons and an internal plane of symmetry, optically inactive by internal compensation.

sections.heading: 7. Lactic acid and tartaric acid; counting stereoisomers
sections.body_md: **Lactic acid**, CH₃CH(OH)COOH, has one chiral carbon: two enantiomers (d and l) and the racemic form (dl). **Tartaric acid**, HOOC–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–COOH, has two identical chiral carbons: **three** stereoisomers (d, l and meso). **Counting:** n different chiral carbons give **2ⁿ** stereoisomers; a symmetrical molecule has fewer, because of meso forms (tartaric acid: 3 rather than 4; 2,3-dibromopentane, with unlike ends: 4).

key_terms.definition_md: A molecule with n different chiral carbons (no symmetry) has 2ⁿ stereoisomers.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling position isomers "chain isomers" (or the reverse); decide from the skeleton first.
- Saying that functional isomers are metamers.
- Using the tube length in cm or concentration in g/100 mL in the specific rotation formula.
- Writing that a meso compound is a mixture of d and l forms.
- Giving four stereoisomers for tartaric acid.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Isomer questions: structure and name (0.5 or 1 mark each) plus the type of isomerism.
- Numericals: formula, substitution with units converted, answer with sign and unit (degrees).
- Compare/contrast questions (external and internal compensation): one mark per distinct point, with an example.

cards.back_md: Different alkyl groups on both sides of the same group: ethoxyethane and 1-methoxypropane.

cards.back_md: Seven: four alcohols and three ethers.
Two isomers in rapid dynamic equilibrium, usually by a hydrogen shift.

cards.front_md: Keto and enol forms of propanone?
cards.back_md: CH₃COCH₃ (keto) and CH₂=C(OH)CH₃ (enol); keto predominates.

cards.back_md: At least one α-hydrogen next to C=O.
No — it has no α-hydrogen.
Rotation about the C=C bond (or in a ring) is restricted.

cards.front_md: Condition for cis–trans isomerism in alkenes?
cards.back_md: Two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon.
Cis: like groups on the same side. Trans: on opposite sides.
No — C-1 carries two identical hydrogens.

cards.front_md: Which is more polar: cis- or trans-1,2-dichloroethene?
cards.back_md: Cis (about 1.9 D); the trans dipole is zero.

cards.front_md: What are syn and anti isomers?
cards.back_md: Geometrical isomers of oximes about C=N; syn = H and OH on the same side.
Light that vibrates in one plane only.

cards.front_md: What does a Nicol prism do?
cards.back_md: Calcite plus Canada balsam: absorbs the o-ray, passes the e-ray as plane-polarised light.
The angle of rotation α of the plane of polarised light.
Clockwise (d, +) vs anticlockwise (l, −).
[α] = α / (l × c), l in dm, c in g mL⁻¹.
Rotation by 1 g mL⁻¹ solution in a 1 dm tube at stated T and wavelength.
A carbon bonded to four different atoms or groups.

cards.front_md: Which of butan-2-ol and propan-2-ol is optically active?
cards.back_md: Butan-2-ol (chiral C-2); propan-2-ol has two identical methyl groups.
Non-superimposable mirror images; equal and opposite rotations.

questions.stem_md: A student working with a C₄H₈ fraction collected from a cracking unit compares but-1-ene with but-2-ene. The type of isomerism between them is:

options.text_md: chain isomerism
functional isomerism
metamerism
position isomerism

questions.solution_md: The carbon skeleton and the functional group (C=C) are the same; only the position of the double bond changes — position isomerism, option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a pharmacy course on drug stability, students are asked which of these carbonyl compounds can exist in both a keto and an enol form. The answer is:

options.text_md: methanal, HCHO
benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO
2,2-dimethylpropanal, (CH₃)₃CCHO
butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃

questions.solution_md: Keto–enol tautomerism needs an α-hydrogen on the carbon next to C=O. Butanone has them; methanal, benzaldehyde and 2,2-dimethylpropanal have none (a, b, c) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A gas chromatograph in a petrochemical plant resolves several C₅ compounds. Which pair of compounds are chain isomers?

options.text_md: ethanol and methoxymethane
butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol
pentane and 2-methylbutane
propanal and propanone

questions.solution_md: Pentane and 2-methylbutane (C₅H₁₂) differ only in the carbon skeleton — option (c). The other pairs differ in the functional group (a, d) or in the position of the group (b).

questions.stem_md: A solvent store in a university holds diethyl ether, C₂H₅OC₂H₅, and methyl propyl ether, CH₃OC₃H₇. These two compounds are:

options.text_md: position isomers
functional isomers
metamers
tautomers

questions.solution_md: Both are ethers (same functional group, –O–) with different alkyl groups on the two sides of oxygen: metamers — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The molecular formula C₄H₁₀O is used in a quiz on isomer hunting, for alcohols and ethers only and ignoring stereoisomers. The number of structural isomers is:
questions.solution_md: There are 4 alcohols (butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol) and 3 ethers (1-methoxypropane, ethoxyethane, 2-methoxypropane): 7 in all — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A fusel-oil sample from a distillery contains alcohols of formula C₅H₁₂O. The number of structural isomers that are alcohols (ignoring stereoisomers) is:
questions.solution_md: The alcohols are pentan-1-ol, pentan-2-ol, pentan-3-ol, 2-methylbutan-1-ol, 3-methylbutan-1-ol, 2-methylbutan-2-ol, 3-methylbutan-2-ol and 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol: 8 — option (a). (11 counts the mirror-image forms as well.)

questions.stem_md: A flavour chemist lists compounds that share the molecular formula of propanoic acid, C₃H₆O₂, but belong to another class. A functional isomer of propanoic acid is:

options.text_md: butanoic acid
propan-1-ol
ethanoic acid
methyl ethanoate

questions.solution_md: Methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃, has the formula C₃H₆O₂ and contains the ester group instead of –COOH — option (d). The others have other formulas (a, b, c).

questions.stem_md: During a spectroscopy lab, a student wants the enol tautomer of propanone, CH₃COCH₃. Its structure is:

options.text_md: CH₂=CHCH₂OH
CH₂=C(OH)CH₃
CH₃CH₂CHO
CH₃CH(OH)CH₃

questions.solution_md: The enol form arises by moving a hydrogen from carbon to oxygen, giving a C=C and an –OH on the same carbon: CH₂=C(OH)CH₃ — option (b). CH₂=CHCH₂OH (a) is an isomer, but not a tautomer.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ethanol and methoxymethane are functional isomers.

**Reason (R):** Natural gas consists mainly of methane.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true: C₂H₆O is an alcohol (–OH) in ethanol and an ether (–O–) in methoxymethane, and methane is the main constituent of natural gas. R has no bearing on A — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Propanone and prop-1-en-2-ol are tautomers.

**Reason (R):** Polythene is made by polymerising ethene.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true: the two forms are in equilibrium through a hydrogen shift, and polythene comes from ethene. The reason is unrelated to the assertion — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol, both found in a fusel-oil sample, are chain isomers.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. They have the same carbon skeleton, with –OH on different carbons, so they are position isomers.

questions.stem_md: Two isomers that are in rapid equilibrium through the shift of a hydrogen atom, such as the keto and enol forms of propanone, show ___.
questions.solution_md: **Tautomerism** (the isomers are tautomers).

questions.stem_md: Match each kind of structural isomerism with a pair of compounds that shows it.

options.text_md: Chain isomerism
Position isomerism
Functional isomerism
Metamerism

match_right.text_md: Diethyl ether and methyl propyl ether

questions.solution_md: The skeleton differs in the first pair (chain). The double bond moves in the second (position). An alcohol and an ether share C₃H₈O (functional). Two ethers have different alkyl groups round oxygen (metamerism).

questions.stem_md: A hydrocarbon dealer is asked to list the chain isomers of C₅H₁₂. Write their IUPAC names and name the type of isomerism.

answer.model_answer_md: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane. They differ in the carbon skeleton (straight, one branch, two branches on one carbon), so the isomerism is chain isomerism.

questions.solution_md: Three names; chain isomerism.

questions.stem_md: Propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol and methoxyethane are all found on the shelf of a stockroom and all have the formula C₃H₈O. Name the type of isomerism between the two alcohols, and between an alcohol and the ether.

answer.model_answer_md: Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol have the same skeleton and group but –OH on different carbons: position isomerism. An alcohol (–OH) and the ether methoxyethane (–O–) have different functional groups: functional isomerism.

questions.solution_md: Position; functional.

questions.stem_md: Define tautomerism, and write the keto and enol forms of propanone.

answer.model_answer_md: Tautomerism is the existence of two isomers, the tautomers, in rapid dynamic equilibrium, usually through the shift of a hydrogen atom. Propanone: keto form CH₃COCH₃; enol form CH₂=C(OH)CH₃.

questions.solution_md: Definition; two forms.

questions.stem_md: Explain keto–enol tautomerism using ethanal, giving the structures, and say why benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO, cannot show it.

answer.model_answer_md: In ethanal, CH₃CHO, a hydrogen on the carbon next to C=O (the α-hydrogen) can shift to the oxygen, giving the enol CH₂=CHOH; the two forms are in dynamic equilibrium and the keto form predominates. Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen: the carbon next to the carbonyl is a ring carbon with no hydrogen to shift, so it cannot form an enol.

questions.solution_md: Equilibrium; structures; no α-H.

questions.stem_md: A compound tested in a food laboratory, at 0.100 g mL⁻¹ in a 2.00 dm polarimeter tube, turns the plane of polarised light anticlockwise by 8.40°. Which statement is correct?

It is dextrorotatory, with a specific rotation of +4.20°

questions.stem_md: What is plane-polarised light? How does a Nicol prism produce it from ordinary light?

answer.model_answer_md: Plane-polarised light has vibrations in one plane only, whereas ordinary light vibrates in all planes at right angles to its path. A Nicol prism (calcite cut diagonally and cemented with Canada balsam) splits unpolarised light into an ordinary ray, which is totally reflected at the balsam layer and absorbed, and an extraordinary ray, which emerges as plane-polarised light.

questions.solution_md: Definition; Nicol action.

questions.stem_md: Define specific rotation. Write the formula, naming each symbol and the units of l and c.

answer.model_answer_md: Specific rotation is the angle through which the plane of polarised light is turned by a solution of concentration 1 g mL⁻¹ in a tube 1 dm long, at a stated temperature and wavelength. [α] = α / (l × c), where α is the observed rotation in degrees, l the tube length in dm and c the concentration in g mL⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: Definition; formula with units.

questions.stem_md: Describe the parts of a polarimeter and explain how it is used to measure the angle of rotation of an optically active solution.

answer.model_answer_md: Parts: a monochromatic source (sodium lamp), a polariser (Nicol prism) giving plane-polarised light, a tube of fixed length holding the solution, an analyser (a second Nicol prism that can be rotated) and a circular scale. With the tube empty or with solvent, the analyser is set for the reference brightness. With the optically active solution in the tube, the plane of polarisation is turned, and the analyser must be rotated through an angle α to restore the setting. The scale reading gives α; the sign shows whether the substance is d or l.

questions.solution_md: Parts; method.

marking_scheme.step: Rotating the analyser to restore the setting gives α

questions.stem_md: What is a meso compound? Why is meso-tartaric acid optically inactive although it has two chiral carbon atoms?

answer.model_answer_md: A meso compound has two or more chiral carbons but also an internal plane of symmetry, so the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image. In meso-tartaric acid, the two halves are mirror images of each other, so the rotation produced by one chiral carbon is exactly cancelled by the other (internal compensation).

questions.stem_md: A teacher asks the class to compare a racemic mixture of lactic acid with meso-tartaric acid. Distinguish external compensation from internal compensation, with an example of each, and say which of the two substances can be separated into optically active forms.

answer.model_answer_md: External compensation: in a racemic mixture (equal amounts of d- and l-lactic acid) the rotation by the d molecules is cancelled by the separate l molecules. Internal compensation: in meso-tartaric acid the rotation by one half of the molecule is cancelled by the other half within the same molecule. A racemic mixture can be separated (resolved) into the d and l forms; a meso compound cannot, as it is a single compound.

questions.solution_md: External vs internal; resolvable only racemic.

questions.stem_md: Tartaric acid, HOOC–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–COOH, has two chiral carbon atoms but only three stereoisomers instead of four. Name the three, say which two are enantiomers, and explain why the number is three.

answer.model_answer_md: The three stereoisomers are d-(+)-tartaric acid, l-(−)-tartaric acid and meso-tartaric acid. The d and l forms are enantiomers (non-superimposable mirror images). The fourth possibility, drawn with the OH groups the other way round, turns out to be the same as the meso form, because the molecule is symmetrical (the two ends are identical) and has an internal plane of symmetry. So there are 3 and not 2² = 4.

questions.solution_md: d, l and meso; symmetry.

marking_scheme.step: Symmetry makes two of the four possibilities identical (meso)

questions.stem_md:
(a) Lactic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH, is optically active. Locate its chiral carbon, name the four groups on it, and state the number of stereoisomers and their names. [2]

(b) Tartaric acid has two chiral carbons. Name its stereoisomers, say which pair are enantiomers and which one is inactive, and explain why it is inactive. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) C-2 is the chiral carbon, bonded to H, OH, CH₃ and COOH. There are two stereoisomers, the d-(+) and l-(−) forms (enantiomers); an equimolar mixture is the racemic (±) form. (b) The stereoisomers are d-(+)-tartaric acid, l-(−)-tartaric acid and meso-tartaric acid. The d and l forms are enantiomers and optically active; the meso form is inactive. It has an internal plane of symmetry, so the rotation by one chiral carbon is cancelled by the other (internal compensation).

questions.solution_md: Lactic acid; tartaric acid.

marking_scheme.step: (a) chiral carbon C-2 and its four groups
(b) three forms named; d and l enantiomers
(b) internal plane of symmetry: internal compensation

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain the terms racemic mixture and meso form. [2]

(b) Compare external and internal compensation. [1]

(c) Find the number of stereoisomers of (i) CH₃CHBrCHBrCH₂CH₃ and (ii) CH₃CHClCHClCH₃, and explain why they differ. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) A racemic mixture is an equimolar mixture of the d and l forms; it is optically inactive and can be resolved. A meso form is a single compound with chiral carbons and an internal plane of symmetry; it is inactive and cannot be resolved. (b) External compensation: cancellation of rotations between separate d and l molecules (racemic mixture). Internal compensation: cancellation of rotations between the two halves of one molecule (meso). (c) (i) 2,3-Dibromopentane has two different chiral carbons and unlike ends (CH₃ and C₂H₅): 2² = 4 stereoisomers. (ii) 2,3-Dichlorobutane has identical ends and is symmetrical: d, l and meso = 3 stereoisomers. The meso form of (ii) makes two of the four possible arrangements identical.
